title: Creatine and Alcohol: Does Drinking Cancel Your Gains?
excerpt: Can you drink while taking creatine? What alcohol really does to creatine loading, muscle stores, hydration, and recovery, plus how to time drinks around training days.
metaDescription: Can you drink while taking creatine? Whether alcohol cancels creatine, plus its effect on loading, hydration, recovery, and training-day timing.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, you can drink while taking creatine, and an occasional night out will not "cancel" it. Creatine works by slowly filling up the creatine stores in your muscles over days to weeks, and those stores drain just as slowly. One evening of drinks doesn't empty them. What alcohol *does* do is work against the things creatine is meant to support: muscle repair, protein building, sleep, hydration, and your ability to train hard the next day. So the real question isn't whether alcohol wipes out your creatine. It's how much drinking, and when, starts to undo the training gains you're taking creatine for.

**The quick rules:** Keep taking your normal daily creatine dose, including on days you drink. Don't skip it to "save" it and don't double up the next morning. Never mix creatine into an alcoholic drink. Keep drinking moderate on training days, and avoid drinking in the first few hours after a hard session, when your muscles are rebuilding. Drink water alongside alcohol and before bed. If you're in a loading phase, the occasional drink is fine, but heavy drinking during that week is a waste of a loading week. And if you have kidney disease, liver disease, or take prescription medication, check with your doctor before using creatine at all.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and sports nutrition guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor, pharmacist, or registered dietitian who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before using creatine if** you have kidney disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, liver disease, or a history of heavy drinking, or if you take medicines that affect the kidneys (such as regular NSAID painkillers, certain diuretics, or some blood pressure drugs). Get urgent medical help if you notice very dark or cola-colored urine, severe muscle pain and weakness after exercise, confusion, or signs of severe dehydration such as fainting or not urinating for many hours.

## Can You Drink While Taking Creatine?

Yes. There's no known dangerous chemical interaction between creatine monohydrate and alcohol. Creatine isn't a drug that your liver has to fight alcohol for, the way acetaminophen is. It's a compound your body already makes (mostly in the liver and kidneys) and gets from meat and fish. Supplementing simply tops up the amount stored in your muscles.

That said, "no dangerous interaction" is not the same as "no effect on your results." It helps to separate the two concerns people actually have:

1. **Is it unsafe?** For a healthy adult drinking in moderation, there's no evidence that combining the two is harmful. The safety concerns are about heavy drinking, dehydration, and existing kidney or liver problems, which we cover below.
2. **Does it hurt my gains?** Moderate, occasional drinking probably has a small effect. Heavy or frequent drinking, especially right after training, can meaningfully blunt recovery and muscle growth. That's true whether or not you take creatine.

It's worth being upfront about one thing: as far as we know, there's no well-designed human trial that directly tests whether alcohol reduces how much creatine your muscles store. What follows is built from what we *do* know about how creatine works, how alcohol affects muscle and recovery, and the sports nutrition research on each. Where we're reasoning from mechanism rather than direct evidence, we'll say so.

## How Creatine Actually Works (and Why One Night Doesn't Undo It)

To understand why a drink doesn't "cancel" creatine, it helps to know what creatine is doing.

Your muscles store creatine mostly as **phosphocreatine**. During short, hard efforts, like a heavy set of squats, a sprint, or a jump, phosphocreatine rapidly regenerates ATP, the molecule your muscles burn for energy. More stored phosphocreatine means you can squeeze out an extra rep or two, recover a bit faster between sets, and over weeks, do more total work. That extra work is a big part of why creatine users tend to gain more strength and lean mass in studies.

The key point is that creatine works through **saturation**, not through a daily hit. It isn't like caffeine, which acts within an hour and wears off. You build up your muscle stores and then keep them topped up.

### Loading vs. a steady daily dose

There are two common ways to reach full stores, both described in the International Society of Sports Nutrition's 2017 position stand on creatine (published in the *Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition*):

| Approach | How it works | Time to full stores |
|---|---|---|
| **Loading** | About 20 g a day (often 0.3 g per kg of body weight), split into four doses of about 5 g, for 5 to 7 days, then 3 to 5 g a day | About a week |
| **No loading** | 3 to 5 g a day from the start | About 3 to 4 weeks |

Both end up in the same place. Loading just gets you there faster.

### How slowly creatine stores drain

Here's why a night out doesn't wipe your progress. Classic research on creatine supplementation (including the Hultman group's work published in the *Journal of Applied Physiology* in 1996) found that once people stopped supplementing, muscle creatine took roughly four to six weeks to drift back to its starting level. Your stores don't fall off a cliff because you missed a day, or because you drank.

So if someone tells you alcohol "flushes out" or "cancels" your creatine, that isn't how it works. At worst, heavy drinking could plausibly make it a little harder to top up your stores efficiently on that day. It doesn't erase weeks of saturation.

## Does Alcohol Cancel Creatine?

No. Let's take the common versions of this worry one at a time.

**"Alcohol flushes creatine out of your body."** Alcohol makes you pee more, but that's mostly water. Your muscles hold creatine inside the cells, bound up as phosphocreatine. It isn't sitting in your bloodstream waiting to be washed away. Your body does steadily break down a small amount of creatine into creatinine every day, which your kidneys clear, but that happens whether you drink or not. There's no evidence that a night of drinking dramatically speeds it up.

**"Alcohol stops creatine from being absorbed."** There's no direct human evidence for this. Creatine monohydrate is absorbed very well from the gut, and muscles pull it in through a dedicated creatine transporter. Insulin seems to help that process, which is why some studies have found that taking creatine with a carbohydrate-rich meal increases how much the muscles retain. Heavy drinking can disrupt blood sugar and appetite, and it can irritate the gut, so it's reasonable to think a very heavy night isn't an ideal setting for a dose. But "not ideal" is very different from "cancelled."

**"Alcohol and creatine together damage your kidneys."** This one deserves a fuller answer, and it's covered in its own section below. The short version: for healthy people, the research on creatine and kidney function is reassuring, and the bigger concern with heavy drinking is dehydration and its effect on the kidneys, not the creatine itself.

**"If I drink, I should skip creatine that day."** There's no reason to. Skipping a dose just means one less day of topping up. Keep your routine steady.

## The Real Problem: Alcohol Works Against What Creatine Supports

If creatine isn't cancelled, why do people feel worse about their training after drinking? Because alcohol interferes with several of the processes that turn training plus creatine into actual results.

### 1. Muscle protein synthesis

Muscle growth depends on your body building new muscle protein after training. One of the most cited studies on this is a 2014 trial by Parr and colleagues, published in *PLOS ONE*. Physically active men did a combined session of resistance training, cycling intervals, and steady cycling, then drank a large amount of alcohol (roughly 1.5 g per kg of body weight, which is a binge-level amount for most people) over the following hours. Muscle protein synthesis was clearly lower than when they had the same session without alcohol. Eating protein alongside the alcohol reduced the damage but did not fully restore it.

Two caveats matter here. First, the dose was large: for an 80 kg person, it's something like 10 or more standard drinks. Second, it was a small study in young men. It doesn't tell us that a beer after the gym ruins your session. It does show that heavy drinking right after training works directly against muscle building. We go deeper into this in our guide to [alcohol, protein synthesis, and muscle recovery](/never-hungover/alcohol-protein-synthesis-muscle-recovery-impact-guide-2025).

### 2. Recovery and strength the next day

Research from Massey University in New Zealand, led by Matthew Barnes and published around 2010, looked at what happens when people drink a moderate-to-large amount of alcohol after a muscle-damaging workout (hard eccentric exercise, where the muscle lengthens under load). Those who drank lost more strength in the days after than those who didn't. Again, the doses used were well above "one or two drinks," and smaller amounts haven't shown the same clear effect.

For creatine users, this matters because one of creatine's benefits is helping you recover between sessions so you can train hard again. If alcohol leaves you weaker and sorer, you're partly working against that benefit.

### 3. Sleep

Alcohol can help you fall asleep faster, but it tends to break up sleep in the second half of the night and suppress REM sleep. Poor sleep reduces training quality and recovery, and it's one of the main reasons a "few drinks" can leave you flat at the gym the next morning. If you want the detail, our article on [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025) explains what's going on.

### 4. Hormones and appetite

Heavy drinking can temporarily lower testosterone and raise cortisol, though the effects of moderate drinking appear small and short-lived. Alcohol also adds a lot of calories with no protein, and it often leads to late-night food choices that don't fit a training plan. If your goal is building lean mass or cutting fat, those calories matter as much as anything else in this article.

### 5. Training quality

Hangovers lower performance. Even when you don't feel terrible, reaction time, coordination, and power output can all be off the morning after a heavy night. Creatine helps you do more high-intensity work, but only if you're actually able to do the work.

## Hydration: The Creatine and Alcohol Overlap Everyone Worries About

Hydration is where most of the confusion about creatine and alcohol comes from, so it's worth getting right.

### What alcohol does

Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, also called antidiuretic hormone. That's the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of it around, you urinate more than you otherwise would, especially as your blood alcohol rises. Strong drinks increase this effect more than weak ones. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the practical side of staying hydrated on a night out.

### What creatine does

Creatine draws water *into* muscle cells. That's why some people gain one to two kilograms of body weight in the first week of loading: it's mostly water stored inside the muscle, not fat and not "bloat" under the skin.

For years, gym wisdom said this meant creatine would dehydrate you, cause cramps, or make you overheat. The research hasn't supported that. A 2009 review in the *Journal of Athletic Training* (Lopez and colleagues) looked at studies of creatine and hydration and found no evidence that creatine impairs the body's ability to regulate temperature or fluid balance during exercise in the heat. Studies in college athletes, including work by Greenwood and colleagues in the early 2000s, found that creatine users did not have more cramps or injuries than non-users, and in some cases reported fewer.

### What happens when you combine them

There's no evidence that creatine makes alcohol's dehydrating effect worse. If anything, creatine's water is stored in the muscle, and it doesn't stop alcohol from making you urinate more. The two effects are mostly independent.

What *is* true is that dehydration from drinking can make you feel worse, make training harder the next day, and put extra strain on your kidneys. That's a reason to manage hydration, not a reason to stop creatine. Practical steps:

- Have a glass of water between alcoholic drinks.
- Drink a large glass of water before bed.
- In the morning, rehydrate with water and food. A salty meal or an electrolyte drink helps you hold on to the fluid.
- If you're doing a sweaty session the morning after drinking, start with fluids and keep the intensity sensible.

## Creatine, Alcohol, and Your Kidneys

This is the safety section, so we'll be careful with it.

**Creatine in healthy people.** The ISSN's 2017 position stand and a large body of research have found that creatine supplementation at recommended doses does not appear to harm kidney function in healthy adults. Studies have followed users for months to years without finding meaningful kidney damage.

**The lab-test trap.** Creatine raises your blood level of **creatinine**, a breakdown product doctors use as a quick marker of kidney function. That can make a routine blood test look like your kidneys are struggling when they're fine. If you take creatine, tell your doctor before blood work so they can read your results correctly.

**Where alcohol fits in.** Heavy drinking and the dehydration that comes with it can stress the kidneys, especially when combined with intense exercise in the heat. The rare but serious condition **rhabdomyolysis**, where damaged muscle breaks down and releases proteins that can injure the kidneys, has been linked in case reports to extreme exercise, heat, dehydration, and heavy drinking. Creatine isn't a proven cause, but this is exactly the situation where you don't want to stack risks: a brutal workout, a big night of drinking, and very little water.

**Painkillers add another layer.** Many people reach for ibuprofen or naproxen for sore muscles or a hangover headache. Those NSAIDs can strain the kidneys when you're dehydrated, and their labels warn about stomach bleeding in people who have three or more drinks a day. If you've been drinking and you're dehydrated, rehydrate first and be cautious with NSAIDs.

**Who should talk to a doctor first:** anyone with kidney disease or reduced kidney function, diabetes, high blood pressure, liver disease, or a history of heavy drinking, and anyone taking medicines that affect the kidneys. A five-minute conversation with your doctor or pharmacist is worth it.

## Timing: How to Plan Drinking Around Training and Creatine

You don't need to time creatine to the minute. Research suggests consistency matters much more than timing, and studies comparing pre-workout and post-workout doses have found, at most, small differences. The bigger timing question is when you drink relative to training.

### On a training day

- **Train first, drink later, and leave a gap.** The few hours after a hard session are when your body is busiest rebuilding muscle. Heavy drinking in that window is where the research shows the clearest harm.
- **Eat a real meal with protein after training**, before you start drinking. The 2014 Parr study found protein partly protected muscle building even with alcohol on board. It's not a free pass, but it helps.
- **Take your creatine with that meal.** Taking it with food, especially food with carbohydrates and protein, is a simple way to support absorption, and it gets your dose in before the night starts.
- **Keep the amount moderate.** One or two drinks is a very different thing from a session of eight. The research on recovery harm mostly involves large amounts.

### The day after drinking

- **Take your normal creatine dose** with breakfast and plenty of water. Don't double it.
- **Rehydrate before you train.** If you're very hungover, a lighter session, mobility work, or a rest day may be a better choice than a heavy one. Lifting heavy while dizzy or uncoordinated is an injury risk.
- **Prioritize protein and sleep** that day to help get recovery back on track.

### During a loading phase

Loading is a short, focused week designed to fill your stores fast. An occasional drink won't ruin it. But a loading week combined with heavy drinking is a bit of a waste: you're paying for the stomach upset and the extra water weight that some people get while loading, while working against the recovery you'd want to show for it. If you know you have a big event coming up, either start loading after it or skip loading and take 3 to 5 g a day instead. You'll reach full stores in a few weeks either way.

### Should you take creatine before going out?

There's no specific reason to take creatine right before drinking, and no evidence that it protects you from a hangover. Take it at your usual time, ideally with a meal earlier in the day.

### Never mix creatine into alcohol

Stirring creatine into a cocktail, a beer, or a pre-drink shot is a bad idea. It won't do anything useful, it can upset your stomach, and it makes it harder to keep track of how much you've had of either. Take creatine with water, a shake, or food.

## What About Other Training Supplements?

People who take creatine often take other things too. A few quick notes:

- **Pre-workout and caffeine.** Mixing high-caffeine pre-workout with alcohol can mask how drunk you feel, which tends to lead to drinking more. Don't use pre-workout as a party drink.
- **Protein powder.** Fine to take with or around alcohol. If anything, getting enough protein is one of the best things you can do to protect recovery on a drinking day.
- **Electrolytes.** Helpful for rehydration the morning after, especially if you're training. They don't prevent a hangover, but they help you hold on to the fluid you drink.

## How Much Drinking Is Too Much for Your Training?

There's no single number that applies to everyone, and anyone who gives you one is guessing. What the research and common sports nutrition guidance suggest:

- **Occasional light drinking** (one or two drinks, not right after training) is unlikely to have a meaningful effect on your gains.
- **Regular heavy drinking or binges**, especially in the hours after training, is where you'll see real costs to muscle building, recovery, sleep, and body composition.
- **Frequency matters as much as amount.** One big night a month is very different from several drinks most nights.

If you're serious about training and you find you're drinking more than you'd like, that's worth taking seriously on its own. Our guides on [alcohol and athletic performance](/never-hungover/alcohol-athletic-performance-complete-impact-analysis-2025) and [sport-specific alcohol guidance for athletes](/never-hungover/athletes-alcohol-sport-specific-performance-guide-2025) go into this in more detail.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Some of our readers who train also use DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms. Here's an honest view for the fitness crowd:

- **What it might do:** most of the evidence for DHM comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. Some people find it helps them feel better the morning after drinking, which can make it easier to get back to training. It's promising, not proven.
- **What it doesn't do:** DHM doesn't undo alcohol's effect on muscle protein synthesis, it doesn't protect your creatine stores (they don't need protecting), and it doesn't make heavy drinking compatible with peak performance. It is not a substitute for drinking less.
- **Creatine and DHM together:** we're not aware of any known interaction between them, but there are no studies of the combination either. If you take prescription medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.

If you want to try DHM, two popular options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our piece on [social drinking for fitness enthusiasts](/never-hungover/fitness-enthusiast-social-drinking-dhm-2025) looks at balancing a social life with training goals.

## The Bottom Line

- You can drink while taking creatine. There's no known dangerous interaction for healthy adults, and alcohol does not "cancel" creatine.
- Creatine builds up in your muscles over days to weeks and drains slowly over several weeks, so a night out doesn't erase your progress.
- The real cost of drinking is to the things creatine supports: muscle building, recovery, sleep, and training quality. The clearest harm comes from heavy drinking in the hours after training.
- Keep taking your normal daily dose, with food and water. Don't skip it, don't double it, and never mix it into alcohol.
- Manage hydration with water between drinks and before bed. Creatine doesn't dehydrate you, but alcohol does.
- If you have kidney or liver disease, high blood pressure, diabetes, or take regular medication, talk to your doctor before using creatine, and especially before combining it with regular drinking.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking creatine?**

Yes. For healthy adults, there's no known dangerous interaction between creatine monohydrate and alcohol. Keep taking your normal daily dose, drink in moderation, have water alongside your drinks, and avoid heavy drinking in the hours after training. If you have kidney or liver disease or take prescription medication, check with your doctor first.

**Does alcohol cancel out creatine?**

No. Creatine works by gradually filling your muscle stores over days to weeks, and those stores take roughly four to six weeks to drop back to baseline after you stop taking it. One night of drinking doesn't empty them. What alcohol can do, especially in large amounts, is blunt muscle building, recovery, and sleep, which are the benefits you're taking creatine to support.

**Should I skip creatine on days I drink?**

No. Skipping a dose doesn't protect you from anything and just means one less day of topping up your stores. Take your usual dose, ideally with a meal earlier in the day, and don't double up the next morning.

**Can I drink during a creatine loading phase?**

An occasional drink won't ruin a loading phase. But heavy drinking during a loading week works against the recovery you're trying to support, and some people already get stomach upset while loading. If you have a big night coming up, consider starting your loading phase after it, or skip loading and take 3 to 5 g a day instead.

**Does creatine make alcohol dehydration worse?**

There's no evidence that it does. Creatine pulls water into your muscle cells, and research, including a 2009 review in the Journal of Athletic Training, hasn't found that it impairs hydration or temperature control during exercise. Alcohol does make you urinate more by suppressing a water-retaining hormone, so drink water between drinks and before bed whether or not you take creatine.

**How long after drinking can I take creatine?**

There's no required waiting period. You can take your normal dose the next morning with breakfast and plenty of water. Taking it with food, rather than on an empty and upset stomach, is easier on your gut.

**Is it bad to drink alcohol after a workout?**

Heavy drinking soon after a hard session is the clearest way alcohol hurts training. A 2014 study in PLOS ONE found that a large amount of alcohol after exercise lowered muscle protein synthesis, even when protein was eaten alongside it. If you're going to drink on a training day, eat a protein-rich meal first, leave a gap after training, and keep it moderate.

**Can creatine and alcohol damage your kidneys?**

In healthy people, creatine at recommended doses doesn't appear to harm the kidneys, though it does raise blood creatinine, which can make a kidney test look worse than it is. Heavy drinking and dehydration can stress the kidneys, especially after intense exercise in the heat. If you have kidney disease or take medicines that affect the kidneys, talk to your doctor before using creatine or combining it with drinking.

**Can I mix creatine into an alcoholic drink?**

You shouldn't. It won't help, it can upset your stomach, and it makes it harder to track how much you've had of either. Take creatine with water, a shake, or a meal instead.
